title: Don't wait until you're old
translation: Don't wait until you're old to start on the Buddhist path. Most of the old graves belong to young people. You fall ill when you least expect it, you're suddenly about to die, and only then do you see where you went wrong. And what you got wrong is simple. You took your time over the things that were urgent, rushed the things that could wait, and now you regret how you spent your life. Regretting it then won't help.
So keep it firmly in mind that death is coming for you, and don't forget it for a moment. Do that, and the world will have less of a hold on you, and you'll take your practice seriously.

Long ago there was a monk who answered everyone the same way when they came to talk business, his or theirs: "Something urgent has come up. It could be tonight, it could be tomorrow morning." Then he put his hands over his ears and went on saying his prayers, and in the end he was reborn in paradise. The story is in an old book on how to get there.
Another monk, Shinkai, felt so strongly how short this life is that he never once sat down and got comfortable. He spent his days crouching on his heels.

literal: Do not wait, (thinking) 'when old age comes, then for the first time I will practise the Way'.
Of the old graves, many are those of young people.
Only when, unexpectedly, one falls ill and is suddenly about to leave this world, does one for the first time come to know the mistakes of the time gone by.
The mistake is nothing else: it is the regret of having passed (one's life) being slow in what should be done quickly and hurrying in what should be done slowly.
Even if one regrets it at that time, will there be any use?
People should simply hold firmly in their hearts that impermanence is pressing upon them, and not forget it even for a moment.
Then why would the defilements of this world not become thin, and the heart that works at the Buddha's way not become earnest?

A holy man of old, when people came and spoke of business, their own or others', answered: 'Now I have an urgent matter, and it is already pressing, morning or evening', covered his ears, recited the nembutsu, and in the end achieved rebirth (in paradise): so it is in Zenrin's Ten Causes.
The holy man called Shinkai thought so much about how temporary this world is that he did not even sit down calmly, and was always only crouching.

notes.quote: 古き墳多くはこれ少年の人なり
notes.text: The 1925 edition points to an old Chinese couplet: 莫待老来方学道、古墳尽是少年人, 'don't wait until you're old to learn the Way; the old graves are all of young people'. Kenkō's first two sentences follow it closely.
{道|みち}を{行|ぎやう}ず: to practise the Buddhist way. In this section, 'the way' always means the Buddhist path.
こそ … るれ: the realis form of る closes the こそ. Here る is spontaneous: 'it comes to be known', 'you realise'.
や: a rhetorical question, 'will there be any use? (No.)'. {甲斐|かひ}: 'use, result'. Modern {甲斐|かい}がない 'it's no use' is the same word.

notes.quote: 無常の身に迫りぬる事
notes.text: {無常|むじやう}: impermanence. Here it means death, which is coming closer.

notes.quote: などか此の世の濁りもうすく
notes.text: などか … ざらむ: 'why would it not…? (It would.)'. {濁|にご}り: the dirt of the world, the desires that keep you tied to it.
'It is already pressing, morning or evening': the urgent business is his own death, which could come any day. The answer works on everybody, because it is true for everybody.
{念仏|ねんぶつ}: saying the name of Amida Buddha (なむあみだぶつ) over and over, to be reborn in his paradise, the Pure Land. {往生|わうじやう}: that rebirth.
Ōjō Jūin, 'Ten causes for rebirth (in paradise)', by Yōkan (1033–1111) of Zenrinji, the temple in Higashiyama also known as Eikandō. The 1925 edition gives this identification.

Shinkai, a Pure Land monk of the late twelfth century. Sayings of his appear in Ichigon Hōdan, a collection of short sayings by Pure Land monks, which Kenkō quotes in section 98. ついゐる: to kneel or sit down properly. うづくまる: to crouch, squatting on your heels, the way you sit when you are about to get up again.
